stories.headline: Democratic Sweep of Border Districts and Governorships Creates New Check on Trump's Immigration Policy
stories.summary:
Voters in the midterm elections handed Democrats all 10 U.S. House districts that touch the Mexican border, along with all four border-state governorships: California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas. According to National Governors Association records cited by Axios, Democrats last held all four of those offices in January 1979.

Starting next year, the sweep gives Democrats new leverage over state resources, border spending and legal challenges during the final two years of President Trump's term. Democratic officials in those states will have more room to contest federal enforcement actions and to decide how state agencies cooperate with them. Supporters of the administration's border policies have argued that enforcement priorities were set by a national mandate and should not be impeded by state officials.

The shift comes alongside a separate confrontation in Washington over congressional oversight. White House Counsel Will Scharf said the administration will not commit to complying with potential subpoenas from a Democratic-led Congress, and he suggested that company executives who have had contact with Trump may be covered by executive privilege. Scharf's letter warned that abusive subpoenas could cross into criminality. Rep. Robert Garcia, a Democrat, responded that Trump has something to hide.

The new alignment sets up a likely series of legal and budgetary disputes over immigration enforcement. Fox News and other right-leaning outlets have covered the Democratic gains as a challenge to the administration's agenda, while Democrats describe the results as a voter rebuke of it.

stories.headline: Zelensky Urges US and Musk to Lift Starshield Speed Restrictions as Russia Hits Energy Sites
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said a crucial US satellite internet service is still operating too slowly, hampering Ukraine's ability to stop Russian attacks. "We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," he said, adding that it is important to be "on the right side of history."

The issue involves Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink owned by Elon Musk and provided to Ukraine by the US government. Ukraine uses it to guide interceptor drones against missiles and drones. Zelensky said speed limits of about 100mph have been enforced since Monday in Russian-occupied areas. Interceptor drones lose connection with operators at that speed and cannot catch Russian jet-powered Shahed-type drones targeting electricity substations. He also argued that imposing limits in occupied areas amounts to partially recognizing them as not Ukrainian.

The restrictions were first identified in October and prompted conflicting accounts. Musk said the US government controls Starshield, while Trump denied responsibility and said he had told Musk to "put it back." The dispute coincides with tension between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Trump says have pushed global prices higher and which Kyiv says are vital to cutting Moscow's revenue.

Ukraine also faces a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors. Overnight into Sunday, Russia struck energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said. The BBC asked the White House and Starlink for comment.

stories.headline: Ebola Outbreak in Eastern Congo Has Killed 5,400, Second-Deadliest on Record
stories.summary:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed about 5,400 people and infected 11,000, making it the second-deadliest ever recorded. The World Health Organization declared it a public health emergency of international concern in May. North Kivu province, where the city of Butembo lies, is the epicentre and has the most reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.

Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga, a 30-year-old physician at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, is one of 3,031 survivors. He believes he was infected through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures were inadequate. His family regarded the treatment centre as a "death house," and his mother pleaded with him not to go, but he knew he was unlikely to survive at home.

His case illustrates obstacles to the response. Butembo lacks equipment for rapid testing, so samples must be sent to Beni, 54km away. Poor roads in the war-torn region mean the trip can take 48 to 72 hours, delaying diagnosis. Fear of treatment centres and stigma also hinder efforts to contain the spread.

Kamwanga now speaks publicly about his recovery to encourage people to seek care early, and he is writing a book about the experience. He says survivors are living proof that the disease is real and that recovery is possible.

stories.headline: Sotheby's Says It Is Seeking Resolution Over $180 Million Van Gogh Amid Nazi-Era Sale Claims
stories.summary:
Sotheby's said it is working to resolve a dispute over the planned sale of Vincent van Gogh's "Chataigniers en fleurs" ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom"), estimated at $180 million. The painting is due to be auctioned in New York on Wednesday as part of the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Representatives of heirs of the Fischer family, its prior German owners, say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis. A lawyer for the heirs reportedly told Sotheby's, in a letter cited by The New York Times, that the work was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.

Sotheby's says its research has not established a sale under duress but that it is in dialogue with the family and committed to a "mutually satisfactory resolution." Its provenance record shows publisher Samuel Fischer acquired the painting in 1909, and it passed to his family after his death in 1934. It was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 and went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936. Four other owners followed before this year's sale.

It is unclear whether the sale will go ahead as scheduled. The BBC has contacted the heirs' lawyer for comment.

stories.headline: Estonia to Close Border With Russia Next Month After Blaming Moscow for Sabotage Attempt
stories.summary:
Estonia plans to close its border with Russia next month after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted act of sabotage against a local defense company. Estonian authorities described the incident, a failed arson attempt on a drone maker, as the latest in a string of such episodes across the Baltic states.

The decision marks a significant escalation in the Baltic region's response to what its governments describe as a hybrid campaign of sabotage and intimidation linked to Russia. The available reporting does not detail the exact timing of the closure, which crossings will be affected, or what exemptions may apply for citizens, residents or freight.

The move comes as European governments are already tightening security measures against hybrid threats. Germany's parliament recently granted its intelligence services broader powers, and Russia has pressed for a new European security architecture in its talks with US envoys over Ukraine. Estonia, a NATO and European Union member that borders Russia, has been among the most outspoken governments on Russian sabotage. Further details on the evidence cited by Estonian officials and any Russian response are expected in the coming days.

stories.headline: Czechs Stage Largest Protest Since Independence Against Plan to Change Public Media Funding
stories.summary:
Thousands of people gathered in central Prague on Sunday to protest the Czech government's plan to scrap the broadcast licence fee and fund public media from the state budget. Organizers, the Million Moments for Democracy association, said roughly 400,000 people attended, and the rally is being described as the largest protest since the Czech Republic became independent in 1993.

The coalition government, made up of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties, says the change will not affect editorial independence but wants broadcasters to cut costs. Prime Minister Andrej Babis told the Czech News Agency that "no one wants to control public media, no one wants to dictate to them what they should say and do," arguing the current system is outdated and that much of Europe is moving the same way. France abolished its licence fee in 2022 and Norway did so in 2020. Czech households currently pay 205 crowns a month, about $9.44.

Critics say putting funding under the control of the budget would let politicians stifle media freedom, and have drawn comparisons to Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban. Reporters Without Borders has said political attacks on public and private media have become a hallmark of Babis's premiership. Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month, and protests have continued since. Some demonstrators wore paper hats in tribute to Vecernicek, the animated character who introduces Czech Television's nightly children's stories.

stories.headline: Israeli Strike Kills Hamas Rafah Brigade Commander Samir Abu Younis
stories.summary:
Israeli strikes in the Gaza Strip killed a senior Hamas figure, Samir Abu Younis, commander of the group's Rafah Brigade, the Israel Defense Forces announced on Sunday. The IDF credited an overnight strike in southern Gaza and said he had directed terror attacks against Israelis. Both Hamas and Israeli officials confirmed his death.

The killing of a brigade commander is a notable blow to Hamas's military structure in the south of the territory. The reporting provided does not describe any immediate Hamas response or the circumstances of the strike beyond the IDF statement.

Separately, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration said US air travel would not return to normal schedules until late Sunday, after a nationwide ground stop earlier in the weekend left thousands of flights canceled or delayed. Officials have blamed upgrade work for the shutdown, which was covered in earlier reports.

stories.headline: Poll Shows Gen Z Breaking With Older Americans on Socialism, Israel and Religion
stories.summary:
Young Americans are increasingly breaking with political beliefs long held by older generations, according to an Axios analysis published Sunday. The report argues that neither major party can count on old loyalties to win over a generation willing to depart from past orthodoxies on issues ranging from economics to foreign policy and faith.

A September 2026 Gallup poll found that 57% of Americans ages 18 to 34 view socialism positively, compared with 43% who view capitalism positively. That contrasts with attitudes among Americans 55 and older, who remain far more favorable toward capitalism. The analysis also points to shifting views on Israel and on Christianity among younger people.

The piece notes that the election of Abdul El-Sayed as the first Muslim senator-elect has put debates over Islamism, the Muslim Brotherhood and antisemitism at the center of national discussion. Fox News also carried coverage of the topic, reflecting how the issue is framed differently across the spectrum. Conservative commentators have tended to cast the trends as a warning about ideological drift, while progressives point to them as evidence that younger voters want change in economic and foreign policy. The findings arrive as both parties assess the lessons of the recent midterms.

stories.headline: Three Men Sentenced to Death in Jordan Over Fatal Church Shooting
stories.summary:
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for the October 23 mass shooting at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate. The attack killed nine people and wounded 34 who were attending a Christian funeral at St. George's church in the village of Hmoud. Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men were convicted of committing terrorist acts, possessing weapons, promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation and conspiracy to commit terrorist acts.

The defendants are two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law, who have not been publicly identified. They fled the scene and were arrested three days later after a shootout with security forces in an abandoned house, in which all three were wounded and no security personnel were hurt. Authorities have not said why the attackers chose that church. King Abdullah II had vowed the attack would be met with the harshest retaliation, saying those who think they can divide Jordanians with bullets have no chance in the face of national unity.

The case has had regional consequences. The week after the shooting, Jordan struck what its military called terrorist organisations in Syria's southern Daraa province. Syrian health officials said five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed. Jordan said it had coordinated with the Syrian government, which said it had not been notified in advance.

Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014 and another pause from 2017 until June this year. Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority country.

stories.headline: Update: Megaspeed Launches Internal Probe as Suspected Spy Tied to Ex-Nvidia Chief Is Said to Have Left in 2025
stories.summary:
Singapore-based Megaspeed, the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia, said on Sunday it has launched an internal investigation into its business and retained external legal counsel. The company said Alice Huang, a suspected China spy linked to former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year. It said reports containing assertions about its business, supply chain and global operations were not supported by verifiable evidence.

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive after it emerged that he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang and with one of his employees. Megaspeed is suspected of giving Chinese companies backdoor access to Nvidia chips through its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Nvidia is banned from selling its most advanced chips to China. Megaspeed said it complies with US export control requirements and local rules in every market where it operates.

The scandal has deepened tensions within the Trump administration. On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said several agencies had favoured putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months, but that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's department holds the pen and should be asked about its internal process. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month, and other congressional committees have asked him and his department to preserve all records related to Nvidia and Huang.

China denies that Alice Huang is a spy and warned Washington not to use the scandal as a pretext for a technological blockade on AI. Singapore says it does not enforce other countries' unilateral export controls but expects companies in its jurisdiction to respect them.

stories.headline: White House Won't Commit to Complying With Democratic Subpoenas, Counsel Says
stories.summary:
White House Counsel Will Scharf said the administration will not commit to complying with potential subpoenas from a Democratic-led Congress. He said company executives who have had contact with President Donald Trump may be covered by executive privilege. Democrats are set to take control of Congress after their midterm victories.

In a letter, Scharf warned that abusive subpoenas could cross into criminality. Democrats have pushed back. Rep. Robert Garcia said the stance shows Trump has something to hide. The dispute previews likely clashes over oversight once the new Congress is seated, including inquiries touching Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and the Nvidia scandal, where committees have already requested records.

Separately, Trump will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons during planned talks with Xi and Putin, a spokeswoman said, even as China has not engaged with the US over two Americans it detains despite appeals from Trump and positive signals from Xi. The coming week's economic calendar includes a retail sales report and minutes of the latest Federal Reserve policy meeting on Wednesday.

stories.headline: South Korea's Top Scorer on Tax Accountancy Exam Admits Cheating With Hidden Camera and AI
stories.summary:
Han Won-seok, a 34-year-old who placed first on South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam, has admitted cheating with a miniature camera, a mobile phone and generative AI tools. He confessed in a video posted Sunday on his lawyer's YouTube account and said he had also given a written confession to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency. He scored 397.5 out of 400 in the first round, missing one of 160 questions, which prompted online suspicion.

Han said he photographed test questions with the camera, sent them to an AI and checked the answers on his phone, in both rounds. He had earlier denied wrongdoing but said he changed his mind out of concern for the runner-up and other candidates who passed fairly. He said he cheated to earn money and a job that would make his parents proud.

The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting. The president's policy chief, Ha Jun-kyung, said new anti-cheating measures would be introduced and past offenders tracked down. Anyone found to have used AI to cheat will lose their qualification and be barred from retaking the test for five years. The case has been assigned to police investigators, and it comes days before the annual college entrance exam, after recent cases of applicants using AI glasses.

stories.headline: Update: US-Israel War With Iran Continues After Renewed Strikes, as UN Watchdog Cites Isfahan Access Gap
stories.summary:
The conflict between the United States, Israel and Iran continued this week after renewed strikes, with BBC analysis noting that neither side appears to have a clear exit strategy. The coverage says none of the choices facing Iran's leaders offers a clear path to victory. The war has been running for roughly nine months, and the coverage notes the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei as a reminder of how much Iran's leadership has changed.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly raised the prospect of renewing strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities. Satellite imagery taken in November shows evidence of digging and new buildings at nuclear-related sites, according to the reporting. The UN nuclear watchdog says it has never been able to visit a uranium enrichment plant at Isfahan that Iran announced more than a year ago, and it has said it is increasingly concerned about uninspected enrichment activity.

The conflict is also affecting security arrangements at home and abroad. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is now one of several Trump administration officials living on military bases because of safety concerns. Protesters blocked the entrance to RAF Lakenheath in Britain over conflicts involving the United States.

Supporters of the administration's approach argue that pressure on Iran's nuclear program is necessary and that Washington does not need a deal on Iran's terms. Critics, including many Democrats and commentators on the left, question the war's open-ended nature and its costs. Outlets across the spectrum, from Fox News and the Washington Examiner to NPR and the Guardian, are covering the story, which is expected to dominate foreign policy debate as the new Congress takes shape.

stories.headline: Midterm Voters End Long-Running GOP Dominance in State Legislatures
stories.summary:
Democrats took control of state legislatures that had been divided and weakened Republican dominance in others in this month's midterm elections, according to NPR's analysis. The results end a long stretch in which Republicans held a commanding position in statehouses nationwide. The shift extends the party's gains in the midterms beyond Congress and governors' races.

The issues expected to top the new majorities' agendas include expanded access to health care and new limits on school vouchers. State legislatures set policy on education, health coverage, elections and abortion, so the changes will affect millions of residents directly. Several of the newly Democratic chambers had been split, giving the party its first real ability to pass legislation in years.

Republicans have sought to play down the losses. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Friday that "Politics requires more than simply winning elections," as he described the party's setbacks in the midterm elections. Some in the party have urged introspection, and Republicans point to their continuing strength in many other states and to the ordinary pattern of the president's party losing ground in midterm years.

Democrats say voters responded to their message on the cost of living and now expect results. Party leaders are weighing their next steps after the sweep. The legislative sessions beginning in January will be the first test of whether the new majorities can deliver on their promises.

stories.headline: Update: Microsoft Says Services Fully Restored After Global Outage
stories.summary:
Microsoft confirmed on Saturday that its services were fully restored after a massive global outage earlier in the week. In a post, the company said it had completed its efforts to address the underlying issue and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions. The disruption had affected platforms including Outlook, Teams and Copilot.

The outage hit governments, courts, healthcare services, businesses, airlines and banks in many places. Governments including those of Japan, Singapore and Australia reported that the hourslong episode had disrupted some of their operations. Earlier reporting estimated that hundreds of millions of users were affected.

The restoration marks the end of the incident, though questions remain about the root cause and about how heavily public institutions depend on a single provider's cloud and productivity services. Microsoft has not yet detailed in the reporting what the underlying issue was. The episode follows a separate nationwide flight shutdown earlier in the week, which officials blamed on upgrade work, and renews attention to the fragility of critical digital infrastructure.

stories.headline: Update: New Orleans Port Sues Tanker Owners Over Riverboat Collision
stories.summary:
The Port of New Orleans filed a lawsuit seeking more than $1 million in damages from the owners and managers of the tanker that struck the docked cruise ship American Heritage on Friday. The suit, filed in federal court in the Eastern District of Louisiana, names the M/V Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA and its manager Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd. It alleges negligence and gross negligence, and asks that the tanker be seized and sold to cover costs.

About 129 passengers plus crew were aboard the paddlewheel ship, which ended up on its side and partially submerged in the Mississippi River. Thirty-two people from the riverboat were hospitalized with non-critical injuries and no one was unaccounted for, which officials called a "miracle on the Mississippi." Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said there "seems to be some type of a loss of steering," though the exact cause remains under investigation.

The lawsuit says the port terminal was significantly damaged and seeks money for cleanup, inspections and repairs. Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation. Thome said the tanker's crew were safe and that it is cooperating fully with authorities.
